title: Sunsets in Menorca
h1: Sunsets in Menorca
description: The 9 best viewpoints to watch the sunset in Menorca: lighthouses and cliffs with tips from a local guide.
og_description: The 9 best viewpoints to watch the sunset in Menorca: lighthouses and cliffs with tips from a local guide.

blocks.x: Menorca has sunsets that stick in your memory. Beyond the famous beaches, there are discreet viewpoints, lighthouses and cliffs where the sky lights up with oranges and violets. I’m **Daniel Vaquera**, official local guide for Voyager Menorca, and here are my 9 favorite places —with practical tips, recommended wind and little tricks— so you can enjoy the sunset like a Menorcan.
When and how to best enjoy it

x: **Arrive 40–50 minutes early.** The good colors start before the sun touches the horizon and explode 10–15 minutes after sunset.
**Watch the wind.** If **tramontana (N)** is blowing, the north is clearer; with **migjorn (S)**, the south coast feels friendlier.
**Safety and respect.** Closed shoes, flashlight for the return, and always away from the edge of the cliff. Leave no trace: Menorca is a [Biosphere Reserve](/en/menorca-biosphere-reserve/).

blocks.x: 1) Pont d’en Gil (Ciutadella)

x: **Why go:** a perfect natural arch to see how the sun “hides” behind the rock.
**Access:** park near Camí de sa Farola and follow the path (10–15 min).
**Local tip:** stay 10 minutes after sunset; the sky turns magenta and the arch silhouettes the scene like a painting.

blocks.x: 2) Punta Nati Lighthouse (Ciutadella)

x: **Why go:** lunar landscape, silence and a clear horizon to the northwest. The lighthouse was built in 1913 after the shipwreck of the *Général Chanzy*; you can find the full story in the [lighthouse guide](/en/guia-faros-menorca/).
**Access:** narrow road; arrive early to park in the designated area.
**Local tip:** take a jacket even in summer; the wind here is deceiving.

blocks.x: 3) Cala Morell Viewpoints (Ciutadella)

x: **Why go:** dramatic cliffs and white houses that are tinged with gold.
**Access:** several natural terraces signposted above the development.
**Local tip:** lean out (with caution) to the north end; there are usually fewer people and the angle is beautiful.

blocks.x: 4) Cala en Brut (Ciutadella)

x: **Why go:** rock platforms over an intense blue fjord.
**Access:** easy from the development; ideal if you want to take a last evening swim.
**Local tip:** find a low platform for reflections of “liquid gold” in the water.

blocks.x: 5) Artrutx Lighthouse (Cap d’Artrutx – Ciutadella)

x: **Why go:** iconic lighthouse with the sun setting to the southwest and views of Mallorca on clear days.
**Access:** fully paved road; nearby cafeteria.

**Local tip:** ideal for families or if you want a “comfortable” sunset with a chair and a drink. This is the option we recommend in [Menorca with children](/en/menorca-con-ninos-en-un-dia-ciutadella/).

blocks.x: 6) Cavalleria Lighthouse (Es Mercadal)

x: **Why go:** the highest cliff in the north and a 180° panoramic view.
**Access:** road to the lighthouse; respect designated parking areas.

**Local tip:** explore (staying on the paths) towards the west side to find quieter spots. Combine it with a prior swim at [Cavalleria beach](/en/las-mejores-playas-de-menorca-y-cuales-evitar-en-temporada-alta/).

blocks.x: 7) Port de Sanitja (Es Mercadal)

x: **Why go:** an ancient natural harbor —with a Roman past— and mirror-like sunsets.
**Access:** next to Cavalleria; easy paths.
**Local tip:** bring a tripod if you like photography: perfect reflections when the water is calm.

blocks.x: 8) Cova d’en Xoroi (Cala en Porter – Alaior)

x: **Why go:** the sun sinks in front of a cave hanging from the cliff: a very theatrical experience.
**Access:** paid entrance and limited capacity; it’s advisable to arrive with plenty of time.
**Local tip:** book the sunset pass and look for side balconies to avoid crowds.

blocks.x: 9) Monte Toro (Es Mercadal)

x: **Why go:** 358 m high —the island’s rooftop, with the sanctuary of the Virgen del Toro— to see how all of Menorca changes color, with 360° views.
**Access:** road to the summit; parking next to the sanctuary.
**Local tip:** if there’s airborne dust (calima), the sun turns intense red. Perfect for a telephoto lens.

blocks.x: What to bring (quick list)

x: **Water**, something to snack on and a **flashlight** for the return.
**Light jacket**: even in August it cools down with the breeze.
**Closed shoes** if you are going to cliffs.
**Trash bag**: what you bring, you take with you.

blocks.x: Bonus: sunrises in the east

If you’re an early riser, note **Favàritx**, **Sa Mesquida** or **Es Grau**: pastel skies and total silence. Sunrise in Menorca has a different kind of peace. In [September](/en/menorca-en-septiembre/), with the sun rising later, you don’t even have to get up so early.
Frequently Asked Questions
What’s the best place to watch the sunset in Menorca?
a: It depends on the wind and your plan: Pont d’en Gil and Punta Nati for dramatic scenery, Artrutx for comfort with family, Cavalleria for northern panoramic views, and Monte Toro for 360°.

blocks.x: What time should I arrive?
a: 40–50 minutes in advance. The most intense colors arrive 10–15 minutes after the sun sets, so don’t leave right at dusk.

blocks.x: Is there an entrance fee at any viewpoint?
a: Only at Cova d’en Xoroi (ticketed entrance with limited capacity). The rest are free to access; please respect designated parking areas and paths.

blocks.x: Private Talayotic Excursion in Menorca
UNESCO World Heritage site
Three sites. A history spanning over 3,000 years.

A private excursion to understand how Menorca’s prehistoric communities lived, buried their dead, and gathered. We won’t just see isolated stones: we’ll connect each monument with the landscape and the people who built it.

x: 4 hours | half-day excursion
3 sites | private tour
€240 | per group · entrance fees separate

blocks.x: The three sites on the route
01 · CIUTADELLA
Naveta des Tudons
Menorca’s most iconic funerary monument. Its architecture and the findings from its interior allow us to discuss death rituals in the Bronze Age.
02 · ALAIOR
Torralba d’en Salort
One of the most spectacular taulas on the island. Here we interpret the ceremonial enclosure, the talayots, and the community life of the settlement.

blocks.x: 03 · ALAIOR
Torre d’en Galmés
One of the most extensive Talayotic settlements in the Balearic Islands: houses, talayots, hypostyle rooms, and an ingenious water collection system.

title: A Journey to the past: the Archaeological Sites of Menorca
h1: A Journey to the past: the Archaeological Sites of Menorca
description: Discover Talayotic Menorca (UNESCO) with a local guide: Naveta des Tudons, Torralba, and Torre d’en Galmés. ½ day or full day routes. Easy booking.
og_description: Discover Talayotic Menorca (UNESCO) with a local guide: Naveta des Tudons, Torralba, and Torre d’en Galmés. ½ day or full day routes. Easy booking.

blocks.x: Discover Menorca’s most iconic prehistoric monuments—navetas, talayots, and taula enclosures—with an engaging and informative guided tour led by **Daniel Vaquera**, an official local guide. Ideal for history buffs, curious families, and travelers who want to understand the soul of the island.
[See all excursions »](/en/field-trips/)
What is Talayotic Menorca (UNESCO)?

**Talayotic Menorca** was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2023 for its cyclopean architecture and its exceptional testimony to prehistoric life in the Mediterranean. The site encompasses dozens of sites integrated into traditional agricultural landscapes. If you want the full context—chronology, monument types, and how to visit respectfully—check out our [complete guide to Talayotic Menorca](/en/menorca-talayotica-guia/).

If you like combining archaeology and landscape, I also recommend reading our [lighthouse guide](/en/guia-faros-menorca/) and the [best beaches](/en/las-mejores-playas-de-menorca-y-cuales-evitar-en-temporada-alta/).
Suggested itineraries
½ day option (3.5–4 h)

x: **Naveta des Tudons** – emblematic collective tomb and must-have photo.
**Torralba d’en Salort** – spectacular *taula* enclosure and domestic structures.
Interpretation of the Menorcan **rural landscape** between stops.

blocks.x: Full day option (6–7 h)

x: Includes the ½ day option + **Torre d’en Galmés**, the most extensive Talayotic settlement.
Lunch break (local recommendations from our [restaurant guide](/en/restaurantes-menorca-2026/)) and, if it fits, **sunset**.

blocks.x: Key tour sites
Naveta des Tudons (Ciutadella)
Funerary monument with a horseshoe plan and two superimposed chambers, unique in the world. It is Menorca’s archaeological icon and a quick and photogenic stop.

x: **Visit**: 20–30 min
**Access**: short and signposted path from the parking lot
**Tip**: first or last hour for soft light and fewer people

blocks.x: Torralba d’en Salort (Alaior)
Complex with **talayots**, hypostyle hall and one of the most impressive **taulas** on the island. In season, it organizes special activities at sunset or at night.

x: **Visit**: 45–60 min
**Best**: the monumental taula and the open landscape
**Extra**: *Sunset* / *Starlight* program depending on dates

blocks.x: Torre d’en Galmés (Alaior)
The largest Talayotic settlement in Menorca, on a strategic hill with views and an interpretation center. It features water collection systems and circular dwellings.

x: **Visit**: 60–90 min
**Services**: picnic area, accessible sections
**Tip**: hat and water in summer; ideal with a light breeze

blocks.x: Practical information
Best time
All year round. In summer, first/last hours; in winter, avoid days of extreme wind and mud after rains.
What to bring

x: Closed shoes with gripping soles
Water (1–1.5 L per person) and some food
Sun protection or windbreaker depending on the season

blocks.x: Accessibility
Uneven terrain overall. *Torre d’en Galmés* offers accessible sections and picnic tables. We adapt the pace and stops for your comfort.
Rules

x: Do not climb on walls or touch structures
Drones/tripods: only with permission
Respect signage and private properties

title: The 7 Lighthouses of Menorca
h1: The 7 Lighthouses of Menorca
description: Discover the 7 lighthouses of Menorca: history, how to get there, schedules, and local tips to enjoy Cavalleria, Favàritx, Punta Nati and more.
og_description: Discover the 7 lighthouses of Menorca: history, how to get there, schedules, and local tips to enjoy Cavalleria, Favàritx, Punta Nati and more.

blocks.x: Menorca is best understood by following its lighthouses: **seven sentinels** that tell tales of shipwrecks, science, dry stone, and nature reserves. For centuries, the tramontana storms made the north coast one of the most dangerous in the Mediterranean — just on this coast, **over 700 shipwrecks have been documented since the 14th century** — and the lighthouses were born precisely to put an end to that dark history. This guide is written by **Daniel Vaquera**, official local guide of Voyager Menorca, and tells you the **history**, **how to get there**, if there are **opening hours**, and the particularities of the environment, lighthouse by lighthouse.
In this guide

x: [1. Cavalleria Lighthouse (Es Mercadal)](#faro-cavalleria)
[2. Favàritx Lighthouse (Maó)](#faro-favaritx)
[3. Punta Nati Lighthouse (Ciutadella)](#faro-punta-nati)
[4. Cap d’Artrutx Lighthouse (Ciutadella)](#faro-artrutx)
[5. Sa Farola Lighthouse (Ciutadella)](#faro-sa-farola)
[6. Sant Carles Lighthouse (Maó/Es Castell)](#faro-sant-carles)
[7. Lighthouse of the Illa de l’Aire (Sant Lluís)](#faro-illa-aire)
[🗺️ A route to see them all](#ruta)
[💡 Curiosities](#curiosidades)
[✅ Tips before you go](#consejos)
[❓ Frequently Asked Questions](#faq)

blocks.x: 1. Cavalleria Lighthouse (Es Mercadal)
*The oldest standing lighthouse in Menorca, built to curb the wrecks of the north.*
History

Inaugurated in **1857** on cliffs nearly **100 meters** high, at the northernmost point of the island. It watches over the tramontana coast, historically so dangerous that its construction was decided after centuries of documented shipwrecks. In front of it, the islet of **Illa des Porros**; at its feet, the ancient **Roman port of Sanitja**, with over 2,000 years of history.
Can you visit? Schedules

The interior of the lighthouse is not open to visitors, but the **Lighthouse Interpretation Center of Menorca**, in the annex building, is open **from mid-spring to autumn** with hours varying by month. Check it the same week of your visit.
How to get there
Narrow road from Es Mercadal towards Cap de Cavalleria, between dry stone walls and meadows. Parking near the lighthouse and marked paths.
Environment and tips

x: Very close, the beaches of **Cavalleria and Ferragut**, with reddish sand.
Watch out for **cliffs without railings** and the wind: on tramontana days, be extremely cautious.

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+de+Cavalleria+Menorca)
2. Favàritx Lighthouse (Maó)
*Icon of white and black stripes in a “lunar” landscape within the s’Albufera des Grau Natural Park.*
History

Designed in 1917 and inaugurated in **1922**, it was the last lighthouse built in Menorca and the **first in the Balearic Islands with a concrete tower**. Its tower of about 30 meters, with the characteristic black spiral stripe, rises over a landscape of **dark slate** that seems from another planet and has made it one of the most photographed lighthouses in Spain.
Can you visit? Schedules
The interior is **not** open to visitors. The surroundings are, respecting the natural park’s signage.
Access
**In high season, access by private vehicle is regulated** and a shuttle bus runs. Check dates and times before you leave.
Environment and tips

x: Unique geology and fragile soils: **do not leave the paths**.
Nearby virgin coves along the Camí de Cavalls (**Cala Presili and Cala Tortuga**) if the wind permits.
Next to the access track, the **Cós des Síndic**: a temporary lagoon that fills after storms and attracts park birds.

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+de+Fav%C3%A0ritx)
3. Punta Nati Lighthouse (Ciutadella)
*Born from a tragedy; today, epic sunsets among dry stone walls.*
History

It entered service in **1913**, driven by the shipwreck of the French steamer **Général Chanzy** in 1910, one of the greatest maritime tragedies on the island, with a single survivor. The French government itself urged marking this coast. The surrounding landscape, arid and almost lunar due to the wind, is unique in Menorca.
Can you visit? Schedules
Interior **no**. The surroundings and viewpoints yes, with marked paths.
Access
Rural road from Ciutadella (6 km) flanked by dry stone walls. **Designated parking** and last section on foot. In summer there may be restrictions at sunset.
Environment and tips

x: Ethnological landscape of **dry stone**, with barracas and ponts de bestiar, gems of vernacular architecture.
On clear days, the silhouette of **Mallorca** is visible on the horizon.
A few km along the Camí de Cavalls: **Pont d’en Gil**, the natural arch over the sea.
Bring a headlamp or flashlight if you return after sunset.

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+de+Punta+Nati)
4. Cap d’Artrutx Lighthouse (Ciutadella)
*White and black striped tower with the most accessible sunsets on the island, opposite Mallorca.*
History

Lit in **1859** according to a project by engineer **Emili Pou**, it is the second oldest lighthouse in Menorca. Its current silhouette dates from **1969**, when the tower was raised to **34 meters** to improve its range. Together with the Capdepera lighthouse (Mallorca), it guards the channel between the two islands.
Can you visit? Schedules
The lighthouse is not open to visitors, but there is a **seasonal restaurant** in the annex building: it’s the only lighthouse in Menorca with tourist use. Reservation recommended at sunset.
How to get there
Easy access through the Cap d’Artrutx urbanization, next to Cala en Bosch. Parking in the area.
Environment and tips

x: Urbanized area with services: the most comfortable option with children or reduced mobility.
Excellent for **sunset** with the calm sea and Mallorca in the background.

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+Cap+d)
5. Sa Farola Lighthouse (Ciutadella)
*The “urban” lighthouse of Ciutadella, at the edge of the harbor entrance.*
History

Built in **1863** to mark the entrance to the port of Ciutadella and **electrified in 1918**, it was one of the first lighthouses in the Balearic Islands with electric lighting. It is the most domestic of the seven: locals from Ciutadella walk to it daily.
Can you visit? Schedules
Interior **no**. The promenade and viewpoints, always.
How to get there
On foot or by bike from the port along the **Camí de Sa Farola** (about 20 minutes), with pine shade and views of the channel.
Environment and tips

x: Accessible and very photogenic walk, ideal at sunset.
The best spot to watch boats come and go… and to understand the **rissaga** of the harbor.

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+de+Sa+Farola+Ciutadella)
6. Sant Carles Lighthouse (Maó / Es Castell)
*The heir of the first lighthouse in Menorca, at the southern mouth of the port of Maó.*
History

The original lighthouse of **1852** was the **first one lit in Menorca**, next to the ruins of Sant Felip castle. Being in the middle of a military maneuvers area, it was demolished at the beginning of the 20th century and replaced by the current concrete tower, about 10 meters, with black and white stripes.
Can you visit? Schedules
**Visits are not allowed**: it is inside a military compound. Only exterior views from public points.
How to get there
Best view from **Cala Sant Esteve** (Es Castell). Access by car and short final walk.
Environment and tips

x: Combine it with **Fort Marlborough**, the **Fortalesa de la Mola**, and the historic center of [Maó](/en/visita-guiada-mahon-menorca/).

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+de+Sant+Carles+Menorca)
7. Lighthouse of the Illa de l’Aire (Sant Lluís)
*The tallest and the most inaccessible: an uninhabited islet, marine reserve, and refuge of the black lizard.*
History and environment

With its tower of **38 meters**, it is the tallest lighthouse in Menorca — and it was the tallest in all the Balearic Islands until 1977. It stands on an islet of barely **34 hectares** off Punta Prima, home to the **black lizard** (an endemic subspecies of the Balearic sargantana) and protected birdlife.
Can you visit? Schedules

The lighthouse is **not** open to visitors and landing on the islet is **restricted**, especially during the breeding season. The usual thing is to contemplate it from **Punta Prima** or on maritime excursions without stepping on the islet.
How to get there
Direct views from Punta Prima beach. Tourist boats operate in season.
Environment and tips

x: Respect the indications of the **marine reserve**.
Binoculars recommended for fauna.

blocks.x: [View on Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Faro+Illa+de+l)
🗺️ A route to see them all

The seven lighthouses can be seen in **one weekend**. Our proposal from Ciutadella: **Sa Farola** and **Punta Nati** on the first day (with sunset at Nati or **Artrutx**), and on the second day **Cavalleria** in the morning, **Favàritx** at midday, and ending at the port of Maó with views of **Sant Carles** from Cala Sant Esteve and of the **Illa de l’Aire** from Punta Prima. If you prefer to see them from the water, boat excursions along the north or south coast offer perspectives that don’t exist from land.
💡 Curiosities of Menorcan lighthouses

x: **There was an eighth lighthouse:** the first of all (port of Maó, 1852) no longer exists; today a beacon replaces it, and Sant Carles inherits its function.
**In the past, lighthouses were only lit from October to April:** in summer they relied on the skill of sailors.
**Favàritx was a pioneer:** first concrete tower in the Balearic Islands (1922), when the material was still a novelty.
**Punta Nati exists due to diplomatic pressure:** France demanded marking the coast after the wreck of the Général Chanzy.
**The area of the northern lighthouses is a Starlight Destination:** far from light pollution, they are some of the best spots on the island for stargazing.

blocks.x: ✅ Quick tips before going

x: **Sunsets:** classics in Punta Nati and Artrutx. Arrive early and bring a windbreaker.
**Summer regulations:** Favàritx and, occasionally, Punta Nati may have regulated access or shuttle buses. Verify the day of your visit.
**Safety:** do not cross fences or approach the edge of cliffs. Flashlight if you return after sunset.
**Environment:** in s’Albufera des Grau do not leave the paths; it is a fragile environment of the [Biosphere Reserve](/en/menorca-biosphere-reserve/).
**Wind and sea:** if the tramontana blows, the north will be rough; consider lighthouses in the south/west.

blocks.x: Do you want to tour the lighthouses with history and without worrying about logistics? We organize **custom private excursions**: [**write to us on WhatsApp**](https://wa.me/34649902301?text=Hola%2C%20me%20gustar%C3%ADa%20informaci%C3%B3n%20sobre%20una%20ruta%20por%20los%20faros%20de%20Menorca.).
❓ Frequently Asked Questions
Can you visit the inside of Menorca’s lighthouses?

As a general rule, no. At **Cavalleria** the Interpretation Center annex opens in season; **Artrutx** has a restaurant in the annex building; **Sant Carles** is a military zone. Favàritx, Punta Nati, Sa Farola, and Illa de l’Aire are enjoyed from the outside.
Which is the best lighthouse to see the sunset?
**Punta Nati and Cap d’Artrutx** are the classics. Arrive early and bring a headlamp if you return at night.
Are there shuttle buses or restrictions in summer?
Yes, especially towards **Favàritx** and sometimes towards Punta Nati at sunset. Check the current regulations the same week of your visit.
Which is the oldest lighthouse?
Of those still standing, **Cavalleria (1857)**. The first of all was the one at the port of Maó (1852), now disappeared.

title: The Best Beaches in Menorca (and which Ones to Avoid in High Season)
h1: The Best Beaches in Menorca (and which Ones to Avoid in High Season)
description: Local guide to choosing a cove in high season. Recommended beaches, those to avoid, and a link to the official access and parking traffic light system in Menorca.
og_description: Local guide to choosing a cove in high season. Recommended beaches, those to avoid, and a link to the official access and parking traffic light system in Menorca.

blocks.x: Choosing the right beach can make the difference between a perfect day and one of traffic jams and full parking lots. Here is a clear and practical guide with recommendations, access information, and a foolproof trick to **avoid jellyfish**: follow the wind… but *in reverse*.

**Check the status of the parking lots before leaving:** 
[Menorca beach parking traffic light system (official link)](https://mou-tmenorca.com/ParkingsPlatges.aspx?IDIOMA=1&IDPUBDALT=9219).
Recommended beaches
1) Cala Pregonda (North)
Golden-reddish sand, islets off the coast and very photogenic landscape. Wild environment without services.

x: **Access:** from Binimel·là, ~25–30 min walk along the Camí de Cavalls.
**Ideal for:** snorkeling and tranquility.
**Tip:** bring *comfortable shoes* and enough *water/food*.

blocks.x: 2) Platja de Cavalleria (North)
Large reddish sandy area, easy to combine with the lighthouse at sunset. Very limited services.

x: **Access:** large parking lot and wooden walkways.
**Tip:** respect the dunes and avoid using clay on your skin.

blocks.x: 3) Cala Pilar (North)
Virgin spot between cliffs and pine forest. One of the most “wild” jewels.

x: **Access:** ~35–45 min walk from the parking lot.
**Tip:** with north wind (tramontana) there may be waves; choose another cove if you are looking for flat waters.

blocks.x: 4) Son Bou (South)
The longest sandy beach in Menorca (about 2.5–3 km), with service areas and quieter areas.

x: **Access:** simple, several accesses and parking.
**Ideal for:** families and long walks.
**Tip:** respect the dune system and use the signposted accesses.

blocks.x: 5) Cala Binibeca / Binibèquer (Southeast)
Small and very transparent cove, near the famous white village.

x: **Access:** comfortable, but it fills up quickly in summer.
**Ideal for:** snorkeling and photography.
**Tip:** go early or late to avoid crowds.

blocks.x: 6) Cala Mitjana (South)
Turquoise waters among pine trees, 100% “Menorca” aesthetic. Mitjaneta is next door (very small).

x: **Access:** easy path of ~15–20 min from the parking lot.
**Services:** there are no beach bars; bring provisions.
**Tip:** arrive early; the shade of the pine forest is appreciated on hot days.

blocks.x: Beaches to *avoid* (in high season)

x: **Cala Galdana:** very difficult to park; it is usually very crowded.
**Macarella:** access by bus during high season.
**Son Saura** and **Cala’n Turqueta:** parking lots fill up before 8:00 AM in summer.

blocks.x: **Smart Plan B:** if there is red on the traffic light, change zones without hesitation; Menorca has equally beautiful and more fluid alternatives.
Anti-jellyfish trick: choose the coast *opposite* the wind
Jellyfish tend to accumulate where the wind pushes. **Golden rule:** if it blows from the north, go to the **south**; if it blows from the south, go to the **north**… and so on with everyone.

x: Dominant wind
Best area
Examples
**North** (Tramontana)
**South**
Son Bou, Binibeca, Mitjana
**South** (Migjorn)
**North**
Pregonda, Cavalleria, Pilar
**East** (Llevant/Xaloc)
**West–Northwest**
Cavalleria, Pregonda
**West** (Ponent/Llebeig)
**East–Southeast**
Binibeca

blocks.x: *Tip:* check the wind forecast in the morning and decide accordingly.
What to bring, no matter what

x: **Water and food:** there are no beach bars in many coves.
**Sun protection:** high SPF cream, cap/hat and sunglasses.
**Comfortable shoes:** dirt/stone paths and walkways.
**Waste bag:** virgin beaches = zero trash cans.
**Towel or sarong** and, if you snorkel, **goggles/tube**.

blocks.x: Quick logistics

x: **Get up early or go late:** you will avoid heat and crowds.

**Check the parking status:** 
[Parking traffic light system (official link)](https://mou-tmenorca.com/ParkingsPlatges.aspx?IDIOMA=1&IDPUBDALT=9219).
**Respect the environment:** do not leave waste or step on the dunes; Menorca is a Biosphere Reserve.

blocks.x: Summary
**Choose the beach according to the wind**, avoid the ultra-famous coves at peak hours, bring **provisions** and check the **parking status** before leaving. With these rules, Menorca always rewards.

title: Total Solar Eclipse in Menorca 2026: Time, Map, and Where to See It
h1: Total solar eclipse in Menorca 2026: times, map, and best locations
description: Exact timings, interactive map, and the best places to see the total solar eclipse in Menorca on August 12, 2026, with safety tips.
og_description: Exact timings, interactive map, and the best places to see the total solar eclipse in Menorca on August 12, 2026, with safety tips.

blocks.x: On **Wednesday, August 12, 2026**, at sunset, Menorca will experience one of the most extraordinary astronomical spectacles seen in Europe in living memory: a **total solar eclipse**. It will be the first total solar eclipse visible from the Iberian Peninsula in over a century, and it won’t happen again from our island for generations. Using official data from the **National Geographic Institute (IGN)** and the **Government of the Balearic Islands (Govern de les Illes Balears)**, this guide brings together everything you need: what an eclipse is and how it works, exact timings down to the second, maps and the best places to watch it, the **official observation zones (ZOO)** and access arrangements, weather, eye safety, photography, mobility, tips for families, children, older people and people with reduced mobility, the most common mistakes, and a complete plan for the day. No rush, no fine print.

blocks.alt: Diamond ring effect at the beginning of totality during a total solar eclipse, photo by NASA

blocks.x: The “diamond ring” effect occurs in the seconds immediately before and after totality. Credit: NASA / Carla Thomas.

**⚡ In 30 seconds.** On August 12, 2026, the total phase will be visible in **Ciutadella from 8:30:16 PM to 8:31:27 PM** (approx. 1 min 11 s, according to the IGN), with the Sun very low, at **about 2° above the horizon**. Menorca will be the **first Balearic island to enter totality** and one of the last Spanish territories to be crossed by the lunar shadow. To see it, you need a **clear western horizon** (western coast) and **ISO 12312-2 certified eclipse glasses** whenever you look at the Sun during the partial phases. The Government has enabled **9 official observation zones (ZOO) in Menorca**. If you go by car to one of the Ciutadella zones, arrive before 5:00 PM: huge crowd levels are expected.

**⚠️ Updated information — August 7, 2026.** In the four official zones of Ciutadella, traffic will be closed from 5:00 PM, or earlier if crowd levels demand it. Vehicle access to Punta Nati will be closed from 8:00 AM. Measures may change: always check official information before traveling.

blocks.x: What exactly is a total solar eclipse?

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon positions itself exactly between the Earth and the Sun, casting its shadow onto the Earth’s surface. It might seem like this should happen every month, with every new moon, but it doesn’t: the Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5 degrees relative to the Earth’s orbit around the Sun, so the lunar shadow almost always passes “above” or “below” the Earth. The three celestial bodies only align with the necessary precision a couple of times a year, and of those occasions, very few produce a total eclipse visible from an inhabited location.

The Moon’s shadow has two parts: a central, dark area called the **umbra**, where the Sun is completely covered, and a wider, fainter outer area called the **penumbra**, where only part of the solar disk is obscured. If you are within the umbra—a narrow band barely a hundred kilometers wide that sweeps across the Earth at high speed—you see a **total eclipse**. If you are in the penumbra, you see a **partial eclipse**, much more common and far less spectacular. Menorca is fortunate to be right within that narrow band of totality on August 12, 2026.

During the seconds when the Sun is completely hidden, its **corona** becomes visible: the faint outer atmosphere of the Sun, normally invisible due to the glare of the solar disk, which appears as a whitish, diffuse halo around the black silhouette of the Moon. It is, according to those who have witnessed it, one of nature’s most awe-inspiring sights.

blocks.x: Menorca’s 2026 eclipse is **total**. It’s the only type that allows you, for a few brief seconds, to look at the Sun safely with the naked eye.
Why this eclipse is so special for Spain and Menorca

The last total solar eclipse visible from Spain took place on **April 17, 1912**; in the Balearic Islands, the last one was on **August 30, 1905**. In any case, more than a century has passed. The 2026 eclipse will be the first total eclipse visible from the Iberian Peninsula and the Balearic Islands in over a hundred years. This will be followed by another total eclipse on **August 2, 2027** (visible as total only from the southern tip of Andalusia, Ceuta, and Melilla) and an **annular** eclipse on **January 26, 2028**, completing the so-called “Iberian eclipse trio.” After the total eclipse of August 2, 2027, Spain will not experience another total solar eclipse until **2053**; the 2028 one will be annular, not total. It is, without exaggeration, a “once-in-a-lifetime” opportunity for the vast majority of us.

What makes the 2026 eclipse unique in our islands is that it occurs practically at sunset. The path of totality travels across the Earth from west to east—from the Arctic, through Greenland and Iceland, crossing the Iberian Peninsula from A Coruña to the Balearics—and reaches Menorca in its final stages, with the Sun already very low on the horizon. Menorca will be the first Balearic island to enter totality and one of the last Spanish territories crossed by the lunar shadow, with the Sun between 1.4° and 2° high depending on the point on the island: the choice of observation site is absolutely decisive, as we will see.

These are the times calculated for the **municipality of Ciutadella de Menorca** (official peninsular and Balearic time, CEST), according to the National Geographic Institute’s viewer. They may vary by a few seconds depending on the exact point on the island from which you observe:

blocks.x: **Duration of totality in Ciutadella: approximately 1 minute and 11 seconds** (IGN data for the municipality; varies by a few seconds depending on the exact point). According to data from the Government of the Balearic Islands, totality begins first in Menorca and progresses south to Formentera (where the first point enters totality around **8:32:49 PM**). It will be slightly shorter than in Mallorca (where it reaches one and a half minutes) but an equally unforgettable moment. Sunset occurs around 8:45:28 PM in Ciutadella; the partial phase astronomically continues after sunset, but is no longer visible from the island. To check the exact time — to the second — at your specific location, the most reliable tool is the official IGN viewer, which allows you to enter any point on the map.
Day schedule, minute by minute
An eclipse afternoon isn’t just the minute of totality: it’s an experience that unfolds over more than an hour. Here’s the approximate script for Menorca’s west coast:

x: Time
What happens and what to do
**Until 5:00 PM**
Arrive at your observation point. In the official zones of Ciutadella, traffic closes from that time (earlier if there are large crowds). Park, set up your chair, locate west.
Active waiting: picnic, check eclipse glasses, prepare camera and tripod.
First contact. The Moon begins to “bite” the Sun. From here on, keep your glasses on whenever you look at the Sun.
Growing partial phase. The light turns strange, metallic; the temperature drops; the sea changes color.
**Moments before totality**
Baily’s beads and the diamond ring appear. Keep your glasses on until the last bright point of the Sun disappears.
**TOTALITY.** When the Sun is completely covered, remove your glasses and look at the corona with the naked eye. Just over a minute you won’t forget.
The first flash reappears: glasses back on immediately.
The Sun sets still partially eclipsed over the sea. End of observation from Menorca… and the beginning of the Perseids night.

blocks.x: The eclipse phases in visual order: partial, Baily’s beads, diamond ring, totality, and sunset. Baily’s beads and the diamond ring occur in the seconds immediately before and after totality (8:30:16 PM–8:31:27 PM in Ciutadella, according to the IGN).
Duration and Sun altitude: why Menorca is an extreme case

In most eclipses, the recommendation is to seek height. Here it is the opposite. The fact that changes everything is the height of the Sun: **during totality it will be approximately between 1.4° and 2° above the horizon, depending on the exact observation point in Menorca**—the lowest in all of Spain; in Ciutadella it is around 2°. For comparison, in A Coruña the Sun will be at 12 degrees and in Burgos at 8. Two degrees is, roughly, the width of two fingers held together at arm’s length.
This has three practical consequences:

x: Any obstacle—a hill, a building, a tree, a boat, even a bank of low clouds—can completely block totality.
The solar corona, which can be up to 3 degrees across, will sit almost “resting” on the sea: a rare and spectacular image.
The sea horizon on the west coast is, literally, the best possible “seat”, because the sea guarantees a clean, unobstructed line.

Before choosing your spot, check the real visibility from that exact point. These official, free tools are essential:

x: **Horitzó Eclipsi 2026** ([horitzo2026.com](https://www.horitzo2026.com)): an app by the Balearic Government and AstroMallorca. It calculates whether the maximum will be visible from your location, taking into account the **real horizon profile** (not just coordinates). Includes a compass and simulation. Available in Catalan, Spanish, English and German.
**IGN Eclipse Viewer** ([visualizadores.ign.es/eclipses](https://visualizadores.ign.es/eclipses)): times to the second for any point on the island, with the eclipse sequence.

**HERMES Viewer** (Ministry of Transport; [official information](https://www.transportes.gob.es/movilidad-sostenible/estudios-movilidad-big-data/el-trio-de-eclipses-solares-y-la-movilidad)): trajectory, duration, and percentage of obscuration overlaid with roads, ports, and airports. Useful for planning mobility.

**Government of the Balearic Islands** ([official eclipse information and restrictions](https://www.caib.es/webgoib/es/-/saber-ne-m%C3%A9s-preguntes-m%C3%A9s-freq%C3%BCents)): with the map of official observation zones (ZOO), regulated traffic sections, and the ECLIPBAL protocol, updated in the days leading up to the event.

**August 2026 Update.** The Government of the Balearic Islands has enabled **26 official observation zones (ZOO)** across the Balearic Islands, **nine of them in Menorca**. They were chosen from over a hundred possible locations, evaluating visibility, accessibility, capacity, parking, and the possibility of emergency services intervention. The Government itself states clearly: **these are not necessarily the best places to view the eclipse**, but rather those where the safety of people can be best guaranteed.

blocks.x: **How I read it, as a local guide.** The ZOOs solve safety and parking issues, not visibility. With the Sun about 2° high and an azimuth of 288° (west-northwest), the four Ciutadella zones—**Cala en Bosc, Cala Blanca, Son Blanc, and Avinguda Los Delfines**—are the ones that best combine the official arrangements with a clear sea horizon in the correct direction. In the zones on the south coast (Son Bou, Sant Tomàs, Talis) and on the Passeig Marítim de Maó, the sunset line is lower relative to the coast itself or the urban area: they are perfectly valid and safe, but it is advisable to **check the actual horizon profile with the Horitzó Eclipsi 2026 app** from the specific spot where you plan to position yourself.

And a recommendation worth more than any list: if you can see it from your own accommodation or from an area you can reach on foot, and you have a western horizon, do it. It’s the safest way to avoid travel, congestion, and last-minute surprises.
The best places to watch the eclipse in Menorca

Since the Sun will be almost touching the horizon, the key is not height but **a completely open and unobstructed western horizon**: no mountains, buildings, groves, or low clouds. All recommended points are in the western half of the island. I’ve grouped them by type for you to choose according to your plan, but keep in mind the [official access arrangements](#afluencia): several of them are regulated on August 12.
Best beaches and coves to watch it

x: **Cala en Bosc (official observation zone):** coast open to the sunset, with a promenade by the sea, bars, and restrooms nearby. The ZOO covers from the promenade car park to the Cap d’Artrutx lighthouse. Parking is ample but will fill up very quickly that day, and there’s little shade left by that time. Traffic will be closed from 5:00 PM, or earlier if crowd levels demand it.

**Cala Blanca (official observation zone):** somewhat less crowded, with an open western horizon from the side rocks of the cove and restaurants in the urbanization itself. The ZOO runs from Clot de sa Cera to Es Mirador restaurant. Street parking is available; it’s advisable to arrive early and walk the last few meters.

**Cala Santandria:** a wind-sheltered cove a few minutes from Ciutadella, comfortable for families, with bars by the sand. It is not an official zone, so there will be no specific arrangements: street parking is limited, and the earlier you arrive, the better your spot.

**Son Xoriguer and the Cap d’Artrutx area:** the southwestern tip of the island, with the Artrutx lighthouse as a reference, a flat promenade facing the sunset directly, and Cala en Bosc services a short walk away. There is usually a sea breeze: pleasant in August, but secure your tripod.

blocks.x: Best lighthouses

x: **Punta Nati Lighthouse (regulated access on August 12):** offers an excellent western horizon, but the official arrangements **close the car park from 8:00 AM** and regulate access via the CF-5 road. Ciutadella also considers it a **risk zone**, along with Cala Morell and Pont d’en Gil, with Local Police control. Do not expect to be able to arrive by car that day. Outside of August 12, it’s still wonderful: it’s on the [Camí de Cavalls](/en/tourist-guide-cami-de-cavalls/) and is one of the darkest areas on the island.

**Artrutx Lighthouse:** at the southwest vertex, with perfect sunset orientation, flat terrain, and relatively close parking. It is within the official observation zone of Cala en Bosc: of the lighthouses, it is the most convenient and the only one with official arrangements.

**Cavalleria Lighthouse (regulated access on August 12):** its cliffs open to the west offer a clear horizon and a spectacular setting, but the **Camí de Tramuntana to the lighthouse (CF-3) will be regulated** that day, as will the Camí de Tramuntana itself at the Me-15 / Me-7 intersection roundabout. The official alternative in that area of the island is Carrer des Tamarells, in Platges de Fornells.

blocks.x: You can read more in our [guide to Menorca’s 7 lighthouses](/en/guia-faros-menorca/).
Best cliffs and viewpoints

x: **Cliffs of Punta Nati and the north coast of Ciutadella:** height and a 180° sea horizon, but affected by the same access arrangements as the Punta Nati lighthouse.

**Pont d’en Gil:** the natural arch on the west coast, one of the island’s most famous sunset viewpoints, but **considered a risk zone on August 12**, with police control. It can be reached on foot from the Cala en Blanes area via a stretch of coast with no shade or services and an open cliff: it’s not the place for a night of maximum attendance. Very close official alternative: **Avinguda Los Delfines**.

**Passeig Marítim de Ciutadella:** flat, paved, and accessible, with clear views of the sea, the port, and the old town in the background, and bars and services nearby. It is not listed as an official zone, but it is one of the busiest on the island: reserve your spot well in advance. The nearest official zone is Son Blanc. See our guide to [9 sunset viewpoints in Menorca](/en/sunset-menorca-9-viewpoints/).

blocks.x: From the sea

Observing the eclipse from the sea can offer a clear horizon, but it requires professional planning. It should only be done with an experienced skipper or an authorized company, after consulting the marine forecast, navigation warnings, and any restrictions that may be established. The Island Council also reminds you **not to anchor over Posidonia meadows**, maintain a safe distance between vessels, avoid risky maneuvers, and plan your return to port in advance, as a very high concentration of boats is expected right at the end of the eclipse.
Archaeological sites

The Island Council will deploy wardens at **Castell de Santa Àgueda** and **Torre d’en Galmès** and other publicly owned sites, to manage access and prevent climbing on talayots, towers, and heritage structures. These are monuments over three thousand years old: they are to be looked at, not climbed.

blocks.x: Sun direction and horizon

At maximum eclipse, the Sun will be towards the **west-northwest, with an azimuth of about 288°**. In practice: stand facing the sea on the west coast and look for the point where the Sun is setting. A compass (or the one in the Horitzó 2026 app) will confirm the exact direction. The day before, at the same time, check that there’s no obstacle (crane, mast, headland) on that line. The Govern carried out an official visibility rehearsal on April 29 and 30 precisely to verify these points: if the Sun was visible at that time on those days, it will also be visible on August 12.
Weather: chances of clear skies

Climatologically, August is one of Menorca’s most stable and driest months, with predominantly clear skies and a low chance of rain. That’s in your favour. But an eclipse this low on the horizon has a specific enemy: **low clouds over the sea**, which can form even if the rest of the sky is clear. Recommendations:

x: Check the **AEMET** forecast and cloud maps in the 3–4 days beforehand, paying attention to low cloud on the sea horizon.
Always have a **plan B** at another point on the west coast that you can move to with enough time, considering the planned traffic restrictions.
Remember that **high clouds** (cirrus) can still allow you to see the event; low clouds are what ruin it.
From the sea there is more room to avoid cloud cover, but only with an experienced skipper or an authorized company (see the “From the sea” section).

blocks.x: Light pollution and Menorca’s Starlight advantage

Menorca has been a **Starlight Reserve and Tourist Destination** since 2019 (certified by the Starlight Foundation), and the whole island is part of a Biosphere Reserve. It has a Night Sky Protection Regulation and **maximum darkness zones**—Punta Nati, Macarella-Son Saura, Cavalleria-Cala del Pilar, Monte Toro, s’Albufera des Grau, among others—with virtually no light pollution.

For the eclipse itself, with the Sun still above the horizon, light pollution is not a decisive factor. But it becomes crucial right after: if you stay at a dark spot on the west coast after sunset, you will have an exceptional sky for the second part of the night (see Perseids, below). Keep in mind that several of these areas have regulated access on August 12.
Access restrictions, attendance, and mobility: the official arrangements

A very high influx of “eclipse hunters” and visitors from all over Europe is expected, in the middle of August and with the island already in high season. The Balearic Government activated the **ECLIPBAL** protocol, within the Territorial Civil Protection Plan, and the security, mobility, and forest protection arrangements have already been published, in coordination with the Island Council and the municipalities. These are the points that most affect you as a visitor.
General restrictions

x: In the **four official observation zones of Ciutadella**, traffic will be closed **from 5:00 PM**, or earlier if crowd levels demand it.

In the **rest of Menorca**, schedules and restrictions depend on each road and municipality. Generally, restrictions on affected roads will apply **between 3:00 PM and 9:00 PM**, although they may be brought forward or extended for safety reasons.
The restrictions **do not affect** residents, essential services, public transport, or duly justified displacements.

x: **Punta Nati Lighthouse (CF-5):** regulated access and **car park closed from 8:00 AM**.
**Camí de Tramuntana:** regulation at the Me-15 / Me-7 intersection roundabout.
**Cavalleria Lighthouse (CF-3):** Camí de Tramuntana to the lighthouse, regulated.
**Monte Toro (Me-13):** road from Es Mercadal to El Toro, regulated.

**Ferreries:** closure of access roads to l’Enclusa and Camí de Tramuntana d’Ets Alocs, with gradual closures (first partial on the Me-1, then at the access to the Binissuès estate and, finally, access only for residents of the Camí de Tramuntana estates and tourist accommodations).

**Sant Lluís:** Passeig de Cap d’en Font closed at both intersections with Carrer del Caló Blanc, and Passeig de la Mar (Binissafúller Roters) at the crossings with Llevant and Tramuntana, **between 7:00 PM and 9:30 PM**.

**Maó:** possible closure of Passeig Marítim from 7:00 PM and restrictions in Binidalí from 6:30 PM; controls in Es Canutells, Es Grau, and other high-traffic points; restricted access to Favàritx and closure of the batteries during the day.
**Ciutadella:** **Cala Morell, Punta Nati Lighthouse, and Pont d’en Gil** are considered risk zones, with Local Police control.

blocks.x: Screens to follow the eclipse without traveling
If you prefer to avoid roads and crowds, several municipalities will install screens: **Ciutadella**, in Plaça des Born; **Alaior**, in Sa Plaça; and **Maó**, at Cinemes Ocimax and in the port.
Parking and shuttle bus

For the **Son Bou** area, it is recommended to access via **Torre Solí**, where a car park will be set up in Torre Solí II with a **continuous shuttle bus between 5:00 PM and 12:30 AM**. This is probably the most convenient option on the entire island if you are not in a hurry and want to forget about the car.

**Practical consequence:** do not rely on a single access point or improvise at the last minute. Measures will be updated in the days leading up to the event based on expected crowd levels, so **check [the official Government information](https://www.caib.es/webgoib/es/-/saber-ne-m%C3%A9s-preguntes-m%C3%A9s-freq%C3%BCents) on the day itself**, and always follow the instructions of emergency services.
How to get there, parking and public transport
How to get to the west coast

Most recommended spots are in the municipality of Ciutadella, at the western end of the island, about 45 minutes by car from Maó airport via the main road Me-1. From Ciutadella, the southwest resorts (Cala en Bosc, Cala Blanca, Cala Santandria) are 10–15 minutes away. That day, allow much more time than usual.
Parking

x: In Ciutadella there is free parking on the Sant Nicolau promenade and the seafront, as well as paid parking (blue zone) in the centre.

If you go by car to one of the official zones in Ciutadella, **arrive before 5:00 PM**, because traffic may be closed even earlier depending on crowd levels. Whenever possible, walk from your accommodation or use public transport.
In natural areas, space is limited and several accesses are regulated: never park outside permitted areas or block roads or emergency accesses.

blocks.x: Public transport

Menorca has regular bus lines connecting Maó and Ciutadella year-round, and in summer there are services from Ciutadella station to the southern and southwestern coves. That day demand will be higher than usual and some lines may be reinforced or reorganized: check updated timetables with the operator. Taking public transport—or using the Torre Solí shuttle bus for Son Bou—and walking the last stretch can save you the parking hassle.
Eye Safety: The Most Important Thing
You should never look directly at the Sun without adequate protection, **except when the solar disk is completely covered by the Moon during totality**.

blocks.alt: Infographic in Spanish on how to safely observe a solar eclipse with eye protection

blocks.x: How to safely observe the eclipse with eye protection. Credit: ESO / B. Tafreshi (twanight.org) / P. Horálek.

x: Always use **certified eclipse glasses** (standard **ISO 12312-2**) whenever you look directly at the Sun during the partial phases. Regular sunglasses, no matter how dark they seem, do not protect: they allow infrared and ultraviolet radiation to pass through, which can damage the retina without you noticing. X-rays, smoked glass, or homemade filters are also not suitable.

Buy your glasses in advance from a reliable supplier: they sell out in the days beforehand. The Govern has reminded the retail sector that only products that meet international standards should be sold.

**Only remove your glasses when the Sun is completely covered and no bright part is visible. Put them back on immediately when the first flash of light reappears.** The times are only indicative: be guided by what you see, not by the clock.
If you use a camera, binoculars or a telescope, they need their **own solar filter** during the partial phase; looking at the Sun through optics without a filter is especially dangerous.
An alternative and completely safe method is **indirect projection**: make a small hole in a cardboard sheet and project the Sun’s image onto another surface, never looking directly.

blocks.x: Eclipse photography
Photographing an eclipse with the Sun at 2° above the sea is difficult and beautiful at the same time. Ideas to get it right:

x: **Partial phase:** a solar filter on the lens is mandatory. Without it, you’ll damage the sensor (and your eyesight if you use an optical viewfinder).

**Totality:** when the Sun is completely covered, remove the filter to capture the corona. Use varied exposures (bracketing) because the brightness range is enormous. Put the filter back on as soon as the first flash reappears.
**With a phone:** solar filter in front of the lens during the partial phase; during totality you can remove it. Lock focus and exposure manually.
**Composition:** take advantage of how low the Sun is to include the sea, a lighthouse or a coastline silhouette. That’s Menorca’s big differentiator.
**Golden tip:** dedicate most of that little more than a minute to **watching**, not to the screen. The live corona cannot be captured in any photo.

Tips for families, children, older people and reduced mobility
For families and children

x: It’s a fantastic educational experience: explain beforehand how the Sun–Earth–Moon system works using a torch and two balls.
**The Government recommends that children under six years of age do not directly observe the eclipse.** For them, indirect projection, a screen, or television broadcast is advised.
Other minors must be **constantly supervised by an adult**, with their own certified glasses throughout the partial phase.
Choose a comfortable spot with nearby services (Cala en Bosc, Cala Blanca, Son Bou with shuttle bus) to have restrooms and shade during the long wait.
Turn the afternoon into a picnic: it’ll make the wait easier and create the memory.

blocks.x: For older people

x: Prioritize points with easy access and little walking: Son Blanc, Avinguda Los Delfines, or Cala Santandria.
A chair with a backrest, plenty of water and sun protection; the wait can be several hours in the heat.
Avoid narrow road accesses and the walking sections of the lighthouses, which are also regulated that day.
The screens in Plaça des Born (Ciutadella), Sa Plaça (Alaior), or Maó port are a very convenient alternative.

blocks.x: For people with reduced mobility

x: The flat and paved official zones of Ciutadella—**Son Blanc and Avinguda Los Delfines**—and the **Passeig Marítim de Ciutadella** are the best options: flat ground, western horizon, and services nearby.
Some Ciutadella beaches have boardwalks; check which ones will keep access that day.
Arrive well before 5:00 PM to secure an accessible parking space nearby, given the special traffic arrangements.
Check [the official website](https://www.caib.es/webgoib/es/-/saber-ne-m%C3%A9s-preguntes-m%C3%A9s-freq%C3%BCents) to see if the observation zones provide reserved spaces.

blocks.x: Mistakes most visitors make

x: **Choosing the site for the landscape and not for the western horizon.** A beautiful viewpoint facing east or covered by a hill is not suitable for this eclipse.
**Assuming an official zone is the best for viewing.** ZOOs were chosen for safety and capacity, not visibility. Check your spot with Horitzó 2026.
**Arriving late.** In the official zones of Ciutadella, traffic closes from 5:00 PM and there are regulated roads: anyone leaving at the last minute may get stuck during totality.
**Counting on arriving by car at Punta Nati or Cavalleria.** Both accesses are regulated on August 12 and Punta Nati car park closes at 8:00 AM.
**Using regular sunglasses.** They don’t protect you. Only ISO 12312-2 certified glasses work.
**Buying glasses on the day.** They sell out; buy them in advance.
**Not checking the actual horizon.** A mast, a crane, or a bank of low clouds can block 2°.
**Watching totality through your phone.** Experience it with your eyes; the camera doesn’t capture what the eye sees.
**Forgetting that it’s at sunset.** Afterwards there’s no margin: the Sun sets. There will be no “second chance” that day.

blocks.x: Historical curiosities: how previous eclipses were experienced in Spain

August 12, 2026 won’t be the first time the Balearics become a global stage for an eclipse. On **August 30, 1905**, a total solar eclipse crossed Spain and was visible as total from the islands. Unlike the 2026 eclipse, that one happened at **midday** (around 12:02 in the Balearics) and totality lasted almost **four minutes**, making it an extraordinary scientific opportunity.

It was a major social and scientific event. Dozens of international expeditions travelled to the mainland and the islands: British and German commissions and the Russian Academy of Sciences. In Burgos, hot-air balloons—the *Júpiter*, the *Urano* and the *Marte*—were launched, and the young engineer **Emilio Herrera** became one of the first people to observe totality from the air, leaving a memorable description of the corona above a sea of clouds. In Mallorca, expeditions set up at the Son Espanyolet Velodrome and the Grand Hotel; factories were even ordered to close during the eclipse so smoke wouldn’t cloud the atmosphere. One of the drivers of the British expedition, G. F. Chambers, ended up observing it **from the sea**—an option that, with proper professional planning, still makes sense 121 years later.

In Spain as a whole, the last total solar eclipse before 2026 was on **April 17, 1912**. Those early years of the 20th century formed a historic “trio” (1900, 1905, and 1912) that the international astronomical community dubbed “the Spanish eclipses.” History rhymes: 2026, 2027, and 2028 form the new Iberian trio.
A Golden End to the Night: The Perseids

The eclipse date coincides almost exactly with the peak of the **Perseids**, the famous August meteor shower. If the sky stays clear and you’re at a dark spot on the west coast—one of the Starlight maximum-darkness zones—you can stay after sunset and enjoy a second astronomical show that same night: two celestial events in a single evening, something truly exceptional. Menorca, as a Starlight Reserve, is one of the best places in the Mediterranean for it.

blocks.x: Frequently Asked Questions
What time is the eclipse in Menorca?

In Ciutadella, according to the IGN, the partial eclipse begins at **7:37:16 PM** and totality runs from **8:30:16 PM to 8:31:27 PM** (with the maximum at 8:30:51 PM). Sunset occurs at **8:45:28 PM**. Times may vary by a few seconds depending on the exact observation point.
How long does totality last?

In Ciutadella, **approximately 1 minute and 11 seconds** (IGN data for the municipality). Menorca is the first point in the Balearic Islands where totality begins, with the Sun between 1.4° and 2° above the horizon depending on the location: the lowest altitude in all of Spain.
What are the official observation zones in Menorca?

Nine: **Cala en Bosc, Cala Blanca, Avinguda Los Delfines, and Son Blanc** (Ciutadella), **Carrer des Tamarells** (Platges de Fornells), **Passeig Marítim de Maó**, and the beaches of **Son Bou, Sant Tomàs, and Talis**. In the four Ciutadella zones, traffic closes from 5:00 PM. The Government reminds that these are the safest and most accessible points, not necessarily those with the best visibility.
Will it get dark in Menorca?
Not completely, since it happens very close to sunset. The sky will darken noticeably, with a twilight tone in 360°, and the temperature will drop, but it won’t be full night.
Do I need to go to a special place or can I see it from anywhere in Menorca?

The entire island is within the path of totality, so technically it can be seen from anywhere. What makes the difference is having a **clear western horizon**, because the Sun will be very low. If you can see it from your accommodation with a western horizon, it is the most comfortable and safest option.
What if it’s cloudy that day?

August usually brings stable skies in Menorca, but no one guarantees it. High clouds allow you to see part of the phenomenon; low clouds on the western horizon could obscure totality. Check the forecast in the days leading up to it, verify your spot with the Horitzó 2026 app, and have a Plan B.
How do I protect my eyes?

With **ISO 12312-2 certified eclipse glasses** whenever you look at the Sun during the partial phases. You can only remove them when the Sun is completely covered, and you must put them back on as soon as the first flash reappears. Sunglasses, X-rays, or smoked glass are not suitable.
Can I take photos with my phone?

Yes, with a solar filter on the lens during the partial phase. You can remove it during totality. Manually lock focus and exposure and prepare your shot beforehand, because totality lasts little more than a minute.
Is it safe for children?

The Government recommends that **children under six years of age do not directly observe** the eclipse: for them, indirect projection, a screen, or television broadcast. Other minors can observe it with certified glasses throughout the partial phase and under constant adult supervision. It is a magnificent educational experience.
When was the last total eclipse visible in the Balearic Islands?

August 30, 1905. In Spain as a whole, the last total eclipse before 2026 was on **April 17, 1912**. After the total eclipse of August 2, 2027, there will be no other total eclipse in Spain until **2053**; the 2028 one will be **annular**, not total.
Will there be traffic cuts or many people?

Yes. In the four official zones of Ciutadella, traffic closes **from 5:00 PM** (earlier if there are large crowds). In the rest of the island, restrictions depend on each road and municipality, generally **between 3:00 PM and 9:00 PM**. Access to Far de Punta Nati (CF-5, with parking closed from 8:00 AM), Camí de Tramuntana, Far de Cavalleria (CF-3), and Monte Toro (Me-13) are regulated, in addition to closures in Ferreries and Sant Lluís. Consult the details in the [official arrangements](#afluencia) section.

**NASA** — [science.nasa.gov/eclipses/safety](https://science.nasa.gov/eclipses/safety/) (eye safety) and [ciencia.nasa.gov](https://ciencia.nasa.gov/eclipses/lo-que-necesitas-saber-sobre-los-eclipses-solares/).

description: Complete Guide to the Camí de Cavalls (GR‑223): history, sections, tips, and safety. Experience Menorca at your own pace with the help of a local guide.
og_description: Discover the Camí de Cavalls tourist guide and explore Menorca in its 185 kilometers of natural and cultural beauty.

blocks.x: The Camí de Cavalls (GR-223) is the historic path that circles Menorca along the coast. It’s about 185 kilometers that pass through pristine coves, cliffs, cultivated fields, lighthouses, and protected natural areas. Today, it is a marked path that can be traveled in stages, on foot or, in some sections, by bicycle.

In this guide, written by **Daniel Vaquera**, a local official guide from Voyager Menorca, you will find a simple explanation of what the Camí de Cavalls is, which sections we recommend if you only have one or two days, how to decide which area to walk in depending on the wind, and what you need to bring to enjoy it safely. The idea is that you can use this text both to organize your own trip and to have a clear foundation if you decide to come with a local guide.

[Why do it with a local guide?](#por-que-guia)

blocks.x: 1. What is the Camí de Cavalls and what is the terrain like?

The Camí de Cavalls is a public path that goes completely around Menorca, following the coastline as much as possible. It has been documented since the Middle Ages as a patrol path to watch over the island on horseback, hence its name. During the 20th century, some sections were located within private farms, but today it has been recovered as a long-distance path (GR-223) and is part of the landscape of the [Biosphere Reserve](/en/menorca-biosphere-reserve/).
The terrain changes quite a bit depending on the area:

x: **North coast:** wilder, with dark rock, ascents and descents, stony sections, and a feeling of open landscape.
**South coast:** gentler paths among pine trees, ravines, white sand coves, and turquoise water.
**East and west:** a mixture of fields, cliffs, lighthouses, and very wide views towards the sea.

blocks.x: It is not a dangerous path if the sections are chosen well and the signage is respected, but it is worth remembering that there are areas with little shade and other sectors where the ground is uneven. That is why it is important to plan a little before leaving.
2. Why do it with a local guide

The Camí de Cavalls can be traveled independently, but many people appreciate going with a local official guide, especially if it is their first time on the island or if they are traveling as a family or in a group. A guide is not just someone who walks in front, but someone who helps you to:

x: **Choose the right section** according to the level of the group, the time available, and the wind and sea forecast.
**Understand the landscape**: history of the path, fauna and flora, dry stone, toponymy, lighthouses, and curiosities of each point.
**Simplify logistics**: starting and ending points, possible transfers, where to park, and how to combine the walk with a swim.
**Walk safely**, avoiding common mistakes such as lack of water, unrealistic schedules, or exposed areas on Tramuntana days.

blocks.x: In addition, a local guide can recommend other plans for the rest of your stay: what to see in [Ciutadella](/en/what-to-see-in-ciutadella-menorca/) or [Maó](/en/visita-guiada-mahon-menorca/), which [Talayotic sites](/en/menorca-talayotica-guia/) to visit, or which [lighthouse](/en/guia-faros-menorca/) is best suited to the day.
3. Recommended sections if you have 1 or 2 days
If you do not want to go all the way around the island, the most practical thing is to choose one or two representative sections. Here are three very complete and easy-to-adapt options.
3.1 Favàritx → Es Grau (northeast)
**Approximate distance:** 8–9 km · **Difficulty:** moderate · **Environment:** “lunar” landscape, wetlands, and wild coves.

The [Favàritx](/en/guia-faros-menorca/) area has dark rock and is part of the Parc Natural de s’Albufera des Grau. The path advances between socarells, low vegetation, and small coves, and little by little it approaches the town of Es Grau, a very protected bay with a wetland and aquatic birds. It is an ideal section to understand the oldest geology of the island.
3.2 Cala Galdana → Macarella / Macarelleta (south)
**Approximate distance:** 4–5 km · **Difficulty:** easy · **Environment:** pine trees, marés cliffs, and picture-postcard coves.

From Cala Galdana, the path advances along natural balconies above the sea, between pine trees and light-colored rock. It is a very pleasant section for families or for those who want to combine walking and swimming. Macarella and Macarelleta are well-known coves: in high season it is advisable to get up early and always follow the access and parking instructions (you have more recommendations in our [beach guide](/en/las-mejores-playas-de-menorca-y-cuales-evitar-en-temporada-alta/)).
3.3 Es Alocs → Cala Pilar (north)
**Approximate distance:** 4–5 km · **Difficulty:** moderate · **Environment:** red clays, golden sand, and a feeling of isolation.

In this section, the north shows its wildest character. There are ascents and descents, sections with stone, and areas very open to the wind. The reward is reaching Cala Pilar, a wide beach of reddish sand surrounded by colored slopes. With good afternoon light, the landscape is spectacular.
4. When to go and how to choose the area according to the wind

One of the keys to the Camí de Cavalls is understanding that the wind rules. It is not the same to walk with a calm sea as with a strong Tramuntana. In a simple way, you can take the following into account:

x: **Spring (March–May):** mild temperatures, fewer people, and lots of flowers. It is an ideal time for hiking.
**Summer (June–September):** it is hot, so it is best to start early, bring plenty of water, and combine the walk with a swim. Access is controlled in some coves.
**Autumn (October–November):** the sea still retains some temperature, there are fewer people, and the sunsets are very beautiful.
**Winter:** perfect for those looking for calm and stormy landscapes, especially in the north. You have to wrap up well and check the forecast.

blocks.x: Regarding the wind, a simple rule is this:

x: With **Tramuntana** (north wind), the north coast is more choppy and can be hard to walk and swim in. On those days it is usually better to go south.
With **migjorn** (south) wind, the north is cleaner and more pleasant.

blocks.x: A local guide checks the forecast every day and suggests the most suitable coast according to wind, waves, and group level. This makes better use of time and avoids surprises.
5. Practical tips: water, equipment, and transportation
Water, food, and sun

x: Bring **at least 1.5–2 liters of water per person**, more on hot days.
There are not always bars or fountains during the route, so it is advisable to leave with water and some light food (fruit, nuts, sandwich…).
In summer, avoid the central hours of the day and look for sections with some shade.

blocks.x: Clothing and footwear

x: Closed shoes with a good sole (trekking shoes or similar). In some sections, the rock can slip if it is polished or wet.
Cap or hat, sunglasses, and high protection sunscreen.
In winter, a light thermal layer and a windbreaker make the difference.
If you want to swim, bring a swimsuit and quick-drying towel.

blocks.x: Access and transport

Many sections of the Camí de Cavalls start or end in areas where you can park, but in some coves access is regulated in summer. There are also bus lines that connect with key points (such as Cala Galdana, Son Bou, or Es Grau) depending on the season.

If you are a group, it is sometimes worth hiring a private transfer to make a comfortable linear route: enter through one point, exit through another, and not have to worry about the car. On a guided tour, we usually review the best combination for that particular day.
6. Do you want us to help you organize it?

At Voyager Menorca, we prepare tailor-made trips along the Camí de Cavalls: short routes for families, somewhat longer days for regular hikers, or combinations of several days for those who want to experience the island on foot. We always adapt the itinerary to the wind of the day, the level of the group, and what you feel like doing most (more landscape, more swimming, more explanation…).

If you are interested, you can [see all available excursions](/en/field-trips/) or [write to us directly via WhatsApp](https://wa.me/34649902301?text=Hola%2C%20me%20gustar%C3%ADa%20organizar%20una%20ruta%20por%20el%20Cam%C3%AD%20de%20Cavalls.) so we can propose a simple and realistic plan based on the days you have and your level.
7. Frequently asked questions about the Camí de Cavalls
How many days do I need to do the entire Camí de Cavalls?
a: The complete route is about 185 km. Most people who do the full tour usually spend between 8 and 12 days, walking between 15 and 25 km per day. If you don’t have that many days, it doesn’t matter: with 2 or 3 well-chosen sections you can get a very good idea of the path.

blocks.x: Is it a suitable path for people without much hiking experience?
a: It depends on the section. The south coast is usually easier, with gentle paths and less loose stone, and that is why it is ideal to start or to go with children. The north coast is more demanding and is recommended for people with some experience or for days when you find yourself with more energy.
If you have any doubts, it is best to start with an easy section and, if you feel good, gradually increase the difficulty.

blocks.x: What time of year is it best to do the Camí de Cavalls?
a: The best time to walk is usually spring and autumn, when temperatures are mild and the island is quieter. In summer it is possible to do it, but it is advisable to get up early, bring plenty of water, and choose sections with shade and the possibility of swimming. In winter the north can be harsh due to the Tramuntana, but it offers very special landscapes for those seeking calm.

blocks.x: Do I need to hire a guide to tour the Camí de Cavalls?
a: It is not mandatory, but it is recommended in many cases: if you are traveling for a short time, if you want to make the most of the day’s weather, or if you do not want to worry about logistics. A local official guide knows each sector very well, knows which section is suitable according to the wind, and can adapt the pace and explanations to the group.

blocks.x: Can it be done with children?
a: Yes, as long as short and simple stages are chosen. In the south there are perfect sections for families, with little unevenness, pine shade, and sandy coves where you can stop to play and swim. With children it is important to bring plenty of water, sun protection, and some food, and plan the walk as a quiet activity, without rushing. You can find more ideas in our guide to [Menorca with children](/en/menorca-con-ninos-en-un-dia-ciutadella/).

blocks.x: Is any special permit or entrance fee required?
a: The Camí de Cavalls is a public path and there is no entrance fee to walk along it. There may be regulations in some car parks and access to coves in high season, so it is advisable to check the updated information before going. In any case, the basic rule is to leave the place as you would like to find it: without garbage and respecting the indications.
